title: Learning to Choose: What Will Guide Me?
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
source: Essential Human Skills in an AI World (jenshew.substack.com), October 23, 2026
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker and Julie Crum continue their series on student AI use by asking what will guide students when instructions run out. Writing from Lipscomb University and Summit Christian School, they argue that explaining rules is necessary but not sufficient, and that students also need convictions they can carry into situations where no one is watching. At Lipscomb, faculty are moving from a 0 to 6 scale toward a traffic light model of green, yellow, and red assignments, applied to whole assignments or to parts of them. At Summit, the aim is to move students from asking what they are allowed to do toward asking what they should do, using prompts on purpose, ownership, honesty, growth, and responsibility. Students write a personal AI Code of Conviction and build a decision tree for when to use AI. The authors ground this in Baxter Magolda's idea of self-authorship and a 2026 study on guided self-assessment, and they note that the study does not show lasting behaviour change.
points: The traffic light model asks first what an assignment is assessing, so green, yellow, and red designations explain the learning each task requires rather than just policing tools.
The shift from "What am I allowed to do?" to "What should I do?" is the central design goal for secondary students.
Five reflection prompts (purpose, ownership, honesty, growth, responsibility) give students a portable check on whether AI is assisting or replacing their learning.
Students draft a personal AI Code of Conviction by turning three to five chosen values into concrete commitments, then test it against realistic scenarios.
The authors are candid that the supporting research does not establish lasting behaviour change, and they frame the work as an approach to explore, not a proven fix.
quotes: As teachers, we can explain our expectations to students, and we absolutely should. Students deserve to understand what is allowed and why. We also want them to develop convictions they can carry into situations where the instructions are less clear, or where no one is watching.

In green assignments, the student can use AI freely, but they have to be able to demonstrate that the thinking remains theirs as they verify what they’ve gotten from AI and disclose their use. In yellow assignments, the student can use AI but they need to designate clearly where they’ve done so, distinguishing AI contributions from their own work. In the red assignments, AI is not used at all because the point of the assignment is doing the work on your own and the thinking that is required.
With our middle school and high school learners, we are also working on developing assignments and a culture that moves our students from asking “What am I allowed to do?” to “What should I do?
The goal is for students to recognize that the same values that guide them in other decisions should apply to decisions about how to use AI.
Marcia Baxter Magolda (2008) describes a process she calls self-authorship: developing the capacity to examine and take ownership of our beliefs while considering the perspectives of others.

They also reported a stronger sense of responsibility emerging through the use of these practices. The study does not establish lasting changes in behavior, but it gives us a useful approach to explore as we help students develop their own ethical frameworks.

Taking ownership of an ethical framework does not mean making every choice alone or deciding that whatever feels right is acceptable. Our choices still answer to the evidence of our learning, the expectations of our courses, and our responsibilities to other people.
